newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's crisis seen scaring off investors.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's crisis seen scaring off investors.

text.p: A battle between security men loyal to Cambodia's two premiers and the reported surrender of Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot were likely to worsen an already bleak investment climate, business analysts said on Thursday.

While the gradual demise of the Khmer Rouge had long been factored into business plans, rivalry between First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and his co-premier Hun Sen over the remnants of the rebel group was expected to intensify and hit investor confidence, they sad.
"The idea that the Khmer Rouge would crumble at some stage had already been written into the market," said an international business consultant who declined to be identified.
"But the shenanigans of the two prime ministers in reaction to that is just re-emphasising that this place is shady and a cowboy town," he said.
"People want to hold off (investing)," he said.
Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen have for months been locked in a bitter feud over power sharing in their coalition with both men striving to bolster their strength in the run-up to elections next year.

The reported surrender of the hated Pol Pot was likely to intensify rivalry between the two premiers as his departure from the political scene would clear the way for either of the premiers to strike political deals with the moderate remnants of his group, political analysts said.
The Khmer Rouge, responsible for the death of more than one million people during their 1975-79 "killing fields" rule, is on the ropes after a wave of defections and splits.

"There's likely to be more destabilisation in the short term as the two parties try to make use out of the situation," said a senior official at a multinational corporation who declined to be identified.
"As an investor who has put in a lot here, we hope this is not a sign of things to come," he said of this week's incidents.
The Cambodian capital was rocked by fighting on Tuesday night as security forces loyal to the two premiers fought a 90-minute battle.
But even before the current crisis, foreign business people found themselves having to court both ruling parties to ensure a smooth ride, and that situation was likely to worsen, the analysts said.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who were forced into an uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993, are expected to oppose each other in elections next year.
Analysts said many blue-chip investors will wait until after the polls to venture into Cambodia.
"What's becoming clearer is those problems are going to get worse now," said the business consultant.
"Why go in now if your contract might get negated after the elections?"
But analysts said that the longer term outlook would be brighter if the Khmer Rouge problem was finally settled and next year's election resulted in just one party in power.

"The Khmer Rouge is at a dead end. To the eyes of business, this is a good opportunity for peace," said Kao Kim Hourn, executive director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace, a local think tank.
"If the political problems eventually calm down, we will have cause for more confidence in Cambodia," he said.
